title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Solar panel cleaning
audience: Owners of small Australian solar panel cleaning businesses who need a base rate, a minimum charge and a per-panel or per-hour decision before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from your own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Choose between a flat per-panel price and a per-hour quote for an array, and set a minimum charge for a short visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A solar cleaning rate depends on the number of panels, the storey and pitch, the access route, whether the roof is safe to walk, the warranty check and the photographs you provide. A standard single-storey array with easy access is a fixed-scope job. An array that needs a difficult access route, or a roof whose condition you cannot judge until you are on it, is harder to price flat. No current solar cleaning rate was found from a government or trade body, so build your rate from your own costs and billable hours. Do not use a per-panel figure from an older article as a rate.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Owners often price as though every paid hour can be billed. Travel, quoting, admin, marketing, training, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate paid hours for a year, then subtract non-billable time to reach billable hours. Jobber puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours (published 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). That is a general range, not an Australian figure, so check your own log against it. If only 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the costs of all 100 hours come from the 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate needed for a fully billable week.

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment and its upkeep, access equipment, water supply, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure. Have a registered tax agent confirm how they apply to your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by billable hours to get the base rate. Review it each quarter and compare it with what clients accept.

instruction.heading: Per-panel or per-hour, and the minimum charge
instruction.body: Housecall Pro (vendor; country not stated) says flat rates suit repeat jobs with a clear scope. Airtasker's Australian handyman guide says hourly rates suit complex jobs and flat rates suit fixed-scope work. A per-panel price is a flat price with a stated basis, so state the array size, storey and access it assumes. Use a per-hour quote when access or roof condition is unknown until the site visit. Set a minimum charge for a short visit, such as a small array or a return visit, that covers travel, access and checking. Contractor+ suggests setting the minimum from the full cost of the visit, divided by one minus the target margin; its figures are illustrative and not used here. No solar-specific minimum charge was found.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, access equipment, water, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income you need, with allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by billable hours to find the base rate.
For each array, decide whether a flat per-panel price or a per-hour quote fits, and state the basis in the quote.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, access and checking for a short visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative only. An owner is asked to price a 20-panel array. The site visit shows the access route is through a narrow side gate and the roof has a steep section that cannot be judged from the ground.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner quote a flat per-panel price, and what should the quote say?
workedExamples.reasoning: The access and the roof condition are not known until the work is started, so a flat per-panel price would hide the risk. The owner quotes for the clean and photographs on a per-hour basis, with an estimate and the access lines stated, or offers a flat price only after the access is confirmed. The owner does not use a per-panel figure from an older article. The access method is checked against the Victorian working-at-height rule before the price is set, and the minimum charge covers the visit.

equipmentAndPpe: Log of paid and billable hours for one month
Price sheet with the base rate, the per-panel or per-hour rules, the minimum charge and the review date

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from an older per-panel figure or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from your own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing every array flat, including arrays whose access or roof condition is unknown.
commonErrors.prevention: Check access and roof condition at the site visit, and quote per hour where the scope cannot be pinned down.

commonErrors.error: Taking short visits at the same price as a full array, without covering travel and access.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, access and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading price statements are prohibited, and a single advertised price should show the total including any fee. The ACCC guidance does not cover minimum or call-out charges. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm the tax treatment of leave, superannuation and business costs with a registered tax agent.
Electrical work is not priced under a cleaning rate. Solar Victoria says a system should be serviced by a licensed electrician. The licence scope for cleaning crews was not researched.
Victoria: the working-at-height rule for roof access was not checked in this draft. Check the Victorian rule with WorkSafe Victoria before you price any roof access.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
Each solar quote states whether it is per panel or per hour, and a minimum charge is stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the per-panel or per-hour rules, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target; do not use an older per-panel figure as a rate.
Use a flat per-panel price only when access and roof condition are known, and set a stated minimum for short visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: A solar cleaning owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for a short solar visit?
options: Because short jobs need travel but no setup time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, setup and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a solar cleaning base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. General range of 60 to 80 per cent billable; not an Australian figure.

Housecall Pro, 'Flat rate vs hourly', https://www.housecallpro.com/learn/flat-rate-vs-hourly/, published 2 February 2025, updated 7 October 2025. Vendor page; country not stated. Supports: flat rates suit repeat jobs with a clear scope.

Airtasker Australia, 'Handyman pricing guide', https://www.airtasker.com/au/guides/handyman-pricing/, last updated 13 March 2024. Supports: hourly for complex jobs, flat for fixed-scope work. Handyman guide, used for the method only.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Supports: minimum set from full visit cost and margin; figures labelled illustrative and not used.
ACCC, 'Setting prices: what's allowed', https://www.accc.gov.au/business/pricing/setting-prices-whats-allowed, last modified 15 July 2026. Supports: misleading price statements are prohibited.

Solar Victoria, 'Maintenance guide', https://www.solar.vic.gov.au/maintenance-guide, updated 17 July 2026. Supports: servicing by a licensed electrician every two years; electrical work is a separate scope.

Work Health and Safety (Managing the Risk of Falls at Workplaces) Code of Practice 2015, https://legislation.gov.au/F2016L00425/asmade/2016-03-30/text/original/epub/OEBPS/document_1/document_1.html, registered 2016. Commonwealth code; not Victorian law. Cited for the height point; the Victorian rule was not checked.

WorkSafe Victoria, news release on falls risks in the solar sector, https://www.worksafe.vic.gov.au/news/2026-08/crackdown-falls-risks-solar-sector, 26 August 2026. Supports: allowing workers onto a roof without adequate protection is unlawful, even with no incident. Aimed at solar; the principle is stated for any roof.
Note: solar-specific rate, hourly and minimum-charge evidence is UNCONFIRMED. The 2016 per-panel figure is not used as a rate. Electrical licence scope for cleaning was not researched.
